newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe urges unity in French polls run-up.
newsitem.headline: Juppe urges unity in French polls run-up.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged his fractious centre-right coalition on Tuesday to mobilise and stay united in the run-up to parliamentary elections early next year.
But within hours of his appeal, his predecessor Edouard Balladur, a fellow-conservative, urged the government to speed up its tax reforms.
Divisions between Juppe's Gaullist RPR party and its coalition partner the UDF have buffeted the government repeatedly over the past year as the premier hit record unpopularity lows.

"For the months to come, what is necessary more than ever to give the country a new start to pull it out of general pessimism is coherence, cohesion and the unity of our coalition," Juppe told RPR and UDF parliamentarians at a reception to mark the start of the parliamentary session.
Urging his audience to prepare for the elections due by late March 1998, the premier pledged to do everything in his power to keep the two parties united.
"Thank you for your political support. It's not always easy," Juppe told his guests, who included one of his foremost critics, National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin.
In the latest barb fired at Juppe, Balladur told a Paris political rally that the government should launch its planned tax reforms and go further with cuts in Value Added Tax (VAT) and income tax.
"I plan to commit myself fully (in the run-up to the elections)...I will always act in liaison with voters and militants of the RPR as of the UDF," said Balladur, a member of Juppe's RPR party.

The government has said it plans to cut 25 billion francs (five billion dollars) from income tax this year, some of which will be clawed back from taxpayers through higher levies on other sources of wealth.
The ruling conservatives united on Monday to reject trade union demands that retirement at 55, conceded to striking truck drivers in December, be extended to other workers.
The issue is shaping up into the next battle between organised labour and the government, against a background of record 12.7 percent unemployment and strained public finances.
